title: Substance and appearance (ST III.75)
hook: Thomas explains transubstantiation: the substance changes while appearances remain
carry: what it is, not how it looks

segments.voice: Yesterday, sacraments as instruments: God the craftsman, the sacrament his tool, each tool doing its own work. Your line was god's tools. What did you handle with care? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-nine.

At a family reunion, an old woman squints across the yard at a tall man with a gray beard and a cane. She doesn't recognize him. His hair is gone, his voice is lower, he's far heavier than the skinny kid she used to babysit. Then he laughs, and she says his name. Everything about how he looks has changed. Who he is hasn't. Hold on to that, because Thomas Aquinas is about to turn it inside out. Today, his account of the Eucharist, and the word he builds it on: substance.
screen: `EVERYTHING ABOUT HOW HE LOOKS CHANGED.` → `WHO HE IS DIDN'T.` → `NOW TURN IT INSIDE OUT.`

segments.voice: Thomas uses two words from philosophy. Substance is what a thing is. Accidents are the features it has: color, size, taste, weight, where it is. Usually the accidents change and the substance stays, like the man at the reunion. Thomas says that at Mass, something happens the other way around. Jesus says at the Last Supper, in the Douay-Rheims, "Take ye, and eat. This is my body." The Catholic Church takes those words literally. So Thomas reasons it through. The whole substance of the bread is changed into the substance of Christ's body, and the wine into his blood, while the accidents remain: the color, the taste, the weight of bread and wine. The Church names this change transubstantiation: a change of substance. Thomas is careful about what it isn't. Christ's body doesn't travel down from heaven and push the bread aside. Nothing moves. It's a change in what is there, not where something goes. Then the obvious question. Why keep the look and taste of bread? Thomas gives reasons. People don't eat human flesh, and it would be horrifying to them; so the gift comes in the form of ordinary food. And it leaves room for faith. Are the senses fooled, then? No, he says. The senses judge appearances, and the appearances really are there. It's the mind, by faith, that knows what is underneath. In John's Gospel Jesus says: "For my flesh is meat indeed: and my blood is drink indeed." Christians understand this in different ways. Orthodox Christians also speak of a real change, without Thomas's terms; some Protestant churches understand the bread as a sign or memorial. Thomas's word asks you to look past how something looks to what it is.
screen: `SUBSTANCE: WHAT A THING IS.` · `THE SUBSTANCE CHANGES, THE LOOK REMAINS.` · `NOTHING MOVES.` · `THE SENSES JUDGE APPEARANCES.` · then, large: `THIS IS MY BODY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray before the Eucharist. Catholic churches keep the Eucharist in a tabernacle, and some leave their doors open during the day. If you can stop in, sit near it for these two minutes, without saying much. If you can't get to a church, sit where you are, and, if you pray, turn your attention toward the nearest tabernacle you know. If you don't pray, look at one ordinary thing near you and ask what it is, beneath how it looks. The bell holds the time.
Substance. What a thing is, beneath the features you can see and touch. For Thomas, at Mass the substance changes while the appearances remain. Today's word.
Your line: what it is, not how it looks. Today, with one person you'd usually judge at a glance, look past the outside once. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics genuflect toward the tabernacle where the Eucharist is reserved, receive Communion at Mass, and some parishes hold Eucharistic adoration, where people sit or kneel in prayer before the host.

fork.setup: you're Thomas. a student says: if this is Christ's body, why does it still taste like bread? are my senses lying? what do you answer?
options: no: your senses judge appearances, which remain; faith knows the substance.
the body has moved in and pushed the bread aside.
fork.reveal: Thomas says the senses aren't deceived, since the appearances are really there. the change is in substance, and nothing moves.

original.note: Latin: a change of substance, the Church's word for the change at Mass.

trapdoor: what you thought: substance means stuff, like a chemical.
what it means: what a thing is, beneath its features. at Mass, Thomas says, the substance changes and the appearances remain.
what a scholar hears: Thomas borrows substance and accident from Aristotle, and denies that the change happens by any local motion.

sources.ref: Summa Theologiae III, q. 75, aa. 2, 4, 5 (with ad 2)

notes: All Aquinas is paraphrased. Check: Christ's body is not there by local motion (III.75.2); the whole substance of bread converted into the whole substance of Christ's body (75.4); the accidents remain, for reasons including that it is horrible for people to eat human flesh, and for the merit of faith (75.5); the senses are not deceived since they judge accidents, and the intellect is kept from deception by faith (75.5 ad 2).
'Transubstantiation' is attributed to the Church (CCC 1376, Council of Trent); no date given.
Other churches: Orthodox speak of a real change without the scholastic terms; some Protestant churches understand the bread as a sign or memorial. Brief and unranked; confirm fairness.
Practice says Catholic churches keep the Eucharist in a tabernacle (reservation; CCC 1379); confirm wording.
Douay-Rheims wording and verse numbering to confirm: Matthew 26:26 and John 6:56 (Douay numbering).
Editor pass: 'at face value' changed to 'literally', since the lesson's point is that the face value (the look of bread) is not the substance.
